pages.text: CPS ASEC Redesign and Processing Changes CPS ASEC Redesign and Processing Changes Skip Navigation Within CPS ASEC Redesign and Processing Changes CPS ASEC Redesign and Processing Changes April 17, 2019 Collected annually, the Current Population Survey Annual Social and Economic Supplement (CPS ASEC) is one of the most widely used socioeconomic surveys, and provides detailed information on income, work experience, poverty, health insurance coverage, and living arrangements in the U.S. In 2014, the CPS ASEC included redesigned questions on income (specifically retirement income) and health insurance coverage, followed by changes in the 2015 CPS ASEC to allow spouses and unmarried partners to specifically identify as opposite- or same-sex. While data from the updated collection methods were released on schedule, data processing changes to take advantage of this new content are now complete. This page shares information regarding these recent changes incorporated in the CPS ASEC survey design and changes to processing methods to improve data quality, and highlights the implications of these improvements for research on families and economic wellbeing in the U.S. The 2018 CPS ASEC Bridge File and the 2017 CPS ASEC Research File provide income, poverty, and health insurance estimates based on these updated CPS ASEC questions as well as a redesigned processing system. pages.text: CPU support & SIMD — NumPy v2.6.dev0 Manual Skip to main content Back to top Ctrl + K System Settings Light Dark Choose version GitHub Collapse Sidebar Expand Sidebar CPU support & SIMD # NumPy supports a wide range of platforms and CPUs, and includes a significant amount of code optimized for specific CPUs. By default, NumPy targets a baseline with the minimum required SIMD instruction sets that are needed (e.g., SSE4.2 on x86-64 CPUs) and uses dynamic dispatch to use newer instruction sets (e.g., AVX2 and AVX512 on x86-64) when those are detected at runtime. There are a number of build options that can be used to modify that behavior. The default build settings are chosen for both portability and performance, and should be reasonably close to optimal for creating redistributable binaries as well as local installs. That said, there are reasons one may want to change the default behavior, for example to obtain smaller binaries, to install on very old hardware, to work around bugs, or for testing. To detect and use all CPU features available on your local machine: $ python -m pip install . -Csetup-args=-Dcpu-baseline="native" -Csetup-args=-Dcpu-dispatch="none" To use a lower baseline without any SIMD optimizations, useful for very old CPUs: $ python -m pip install . -Csetup-args=-Dcpu-baseline="none" For more usage scenarios and more in-depth information about NumPy’s SIMD support, see CPU Build Options .

pages.description: Wales finished bottom of their Nations League group, but boss Craig Bellamy believes his team showed they belong in the top flight.
pages.text: Craig Bellamy: Wales boss takes belief from Nations League campaign - BBC Sport Image source, Getty Images Image caption, Craig Bellamy's Wales seriously tested reigning Nations League champions Portugal in Cardiff By Dafydd Pritchard BBC Sport Wales Published 17 November 2026 Craig Bellamy kept coming back to one word. Belief. His Wales side had just lost a fifth game out of six to finish bottom of their Nations League group. Bellamy would have been forgiven for feeling a little bruised. But there are ways of losing and ways of finishing bottom. Wales were fearless against Portugal, exhilarating in attack and proving they can compete at the highest level of this competition, even as they were beaten 3-2 in Cardiff. And while they were already consigned to the foot of the Group A4 table, Wales' previous performances mean they at least have the back-up of a relegation play-off in March to preserve their top-flight status. "Belief's the biggest one," Bellamy said when he was asked what he and his team had taken from this campaign. "Not just this game, but in general. We are beyond close to this level. We can more than compete at this level. "We demand and want to expect to be. Getting into League A is big for us, but also staying in A is going to allow us to develop. "You can only develop and improve by playing the best teams, and I felt we've taken another shift." Home Menu About Documentation Download License Support Purchase Search About Documentation Download Support Purchase Search Documentation Search Changelog CREATE VIRTUAL TABLE create-virtual-table-stmt: hide A virtual table is an interface to an external storage or computation engine that appears to be a table but does not actually store information in the database file. In general, you can do anything with a virtual table that can be done with an ordinary table, except that you cannot create indices or triggers on a virtual table. Some virtual table implementations might impose additional restrictions. For example, many virtual tables are read-only. The module-name is the name of an object that implements the virtual table. The module-name must be registered with the SQLite database connection using sqlite3_create_module() or sqlite3_create_module_v2() prior to issuing the CREATE VIRTUAL TABLE statement. The module takes zero or more comma-separated arguments. The arguments can be just about any text as long as it has balanced parentheses. The argument syntax is sufficiently general that the arguments can be made to appear as column definitions in a traditional CREATE TABLE statement. SQLite passes the module arguments directly to the xCreate and xConnect methods of the module implementation without any interpretation. It is the responsibility of the module implementation to parse and interpret its own arguments. A virtual table is destroyed using the ordinary DROP TABLE statement. There is no DROP VIRTUAL TABLE
